opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think embodiment is a really interesting question, and my view on it is a bit nuanced. I don't think physical embodiment is strictly *necessary* for general intelligence in the abstract. If you look at the space of all possible minds, there's no fundamental reason you couldn't have a very powerful general intelligence that lives entirely in, say, the world of mathematics, or the internet, or some data network, and never has a body in the way we do.

But if what you want is an AGI that is roughly human-like, one that understands the world the way we do, can communicate with us naturally, and shares some of our intuitions and values, then embodiment becomes extremely valuable. So much of human cognition is grounded in having a body moving around a world of physical objects: our sense of space, causality, objects persisting over time, other agents with goals, even a lot of our metaphors for abstract thought. Language is shot through with that. When we say we "grasp" an idea or something is "over our heads," that's bodily experience bleeding into abstract reasoning.

So you can try to learn all that indirectly from text and video, and the large language models show you can get surprisingly far that way. But I think there's a kind of shallowness that comes from learning about the world purely through the residue of human descriptions of it, rather than through actually acting in it and seeing the consequences. Embodiment gives you a closed sensorimotor loop: you try something, it fails, you adjust. That's a very rich learning signal, and it ties symbols to experience in a way that's hard to get otherwise.

That's part of why I've been interested for a long time in putting AI systems, OpenCog, Hyperon and so forth, into robots, and why I worked with Hanson Robotics on humanoid robots like Sophia. A humanoid body in particular is interesting because it lets the AI participate in human social life: eye contact, facial expressions, sharing a physical space with people. If we want AGI that grows up, in a sense, in relationship with humans, learning our values through interaction rather than just through a rule list, then having it embodied in a way people can relate to is quite powerful.

There's also a practical side. Robotics is hard and expensive, the hardware is still clunky, so I don't think AGI progress has to wait on robotics. You can do a lot in virtual worlds, game environments, simulated bodies, and those give you some of the same benefits more cheaply. My guess is the path to AGI will be a mix: a lot of the cognitive heavy lifting developed in software, with embodiment, virtual and physical, providing grounding, common sense, and a channel for social and ethical learning.

So in short: not mandatory for intelligence in general, but very helpful, maybe close to essential, if we want AGI that understands us and that we can understand, and I think that matters a lot from a safety and beneficial-outcomes perspective too.

r001.rationale: It discusses embodiment and a closed sensorimotor loop, but does not frame the issue as how much sensorimotor bandwidth an AGI needs.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes abstract general intelligence, which need not have a body, from human-like AGI, for which embodiment is described as highly valuable.

r003.rationale: It allows that a powerful AGI might have no body, but does not say that vastly superhuman AGI could be achieved with sensorimotor access much more restricted than a human's.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've gone back and forth on over the years, honestly. I don't think embodiment is strictly necessary for AGI in some fundamental mathematical sense. You can imagine a mind that just lives in a space of mathematical structures or in a purely digital environment and develops general intelligence relative to that environment. Intelligence is always relative to some set of environments and goals anyway, so there's nothing magic about a body in principle.

But I think for the sort of human-like general intelligence that we actually know how to recognize and that we'd want to interact with, embodiment is pragmatically extremely important, for a few reasons.

One is just the structure of the world. A lot of human common sense is grounded in things like object persistence, causality, the fact that you can't be in two places at once, that if you push something it moves. Large language models pick up a fuzzy shadow of this from text, but text is a very lossy compression of what people actually learn from stumbling around in the world as toddlers. So having a system that can actually act and perceive and see the consequences of its actions gives you a much richer basis for grounding abstract concepts.

The second thing is the self. If you have a body, you have a natural boundary between self and world, and you have a natural source of goals and values rooted in maintaining that body and getting things done with it. A lot of what we think of as agency and motivation in humans comes from that. Now, a body doesn't have to be a humanoid robot. It could be a virtual body in a game world, which is a lot cheaper and a lot of what we did with OpenCog in the early days. But something that has to deal with a persistent environment it only partially controls, I think that's valuable for developing the kind of robust self-model you want.

And then the third thing, which is more on the ethics and alignment side, is that if you want an AGI that has anything like empathy or understands human values from the inside, having it share something of the human condition helps. A system that has grown up interacting with people in physical or at least social contexts, that has had to cooperate, that has experienced something like frustration when its arm doesn't do what it wants, is going to have a more intuitive grasp of what matters to us than something that just read about it.

So my current view is that embodiment is one of several complementary approaches. With the Sophia robot and the Hanson Robotics work, part of the motivation was precisely this: give the system a face and a body, let it interact with people, and use that as a data source and a training ground for the cognitive architecture. I wouldn't say you can't get there without it, but I'd bet on hybrid systems, combining neural, symbolic and evolutionary methods, with at least some embodied or virtually embodied components, as the more reliable path to beneficial human-level AGI, as opposed to just scaling transformers on text.

astra-6.text:
I think embodiment is very important, but I wouldn’t say that a physical body is a necessary condition for general intelligence. You have to distinguish between creating an AGI and creating an intelligence that thinks and feels like a human being.

For humans, the body shapes an enormous amount of our cognition. We learn by moving around, manipulating things, interacting with other people. Even our abstract thinking draws on those experiences. So if you want an AI to understand the world in a humanlike way, giving it a body and letting it learn through interaction is a very natural approach.

But that body could be in a virtual world. There are differences between a simulation and the physical world, of course, but the important thing is the loop: you perceive something, you act, you experience the consequences, and you learn. I don’t see a fundamental reason why that loop has to involve a particular kind of physical hardware.

And you could imagine a general intelligence whose experience is primarily mathematical, or whose environment consists of software systems and interactions with people online. Its understanding would be different from ours. It might have difficulty with things a small child finds obvious, while being very capable in other domains.

So I see physical embodiment as a powerful route toward AGI, especially toward AGI that can relate to us and function in our world. I’m much less convinced that it’s the only route.

sol-6.1.text:
I think embodiment is very useful, but I wouldn’t say a physical body is a necessary condition for AGI. I’d distinguish having a particular kind of body from being able to act in a world and learn from the consequences.

For humans, intelligence develops through a very particular feedback loop. We move, touch things, interact with other people, and gradually build up abstractions from those experiences. A lot of what feels like abstract reasoning is connected to that history of perception and action. So if you want an AI that understands the world in a humanlike way, giving it a body is a pretty natural approach.

But that doesn’t mean the body has to be biological, or even physical. An agent in a sufficiently rich virtual world could learn about objects, other agents, and the consequences of its actions. Its intuitions might differ from ours, but that wouldn’t necessarily make it less intelligent.

The interesting question is what kinds of experience let a system develop generalizable understanding. A robot body can provide those experiences, but the body itself doesn’t solve the problem. You still need an architecture that can turn particular experiences into knowledge and transfer that knowledge to situations it hasn’t encountered before.

r003.rationale: It allows that a virtual agent could learn without a physical body, but does not claim that vastly superhuman AGI could use sensorimotor access much more restricted than a human's.
